nameStory: The "winterchill" part of this millipede's common name comes from its remarkable cold tolerance - it's one of the few millipedes that stays active during New England's harsh winter months. The species name "blakei" honors an early naturalist who first collected specimens of this hardy little creature. While most millipedes hunker down when temperatures drop, winterchill millipedes seem to embrace the freeze!
description: Conotyla blakei is a small, slender millipede that's part of the chordeumatid group - millipedes known for their cylindrical, worm-like appearance. Like all millipedes, it has two pairs of legs per body segment (unlike centipedes which have just one pair per segment). These creatures are decomposers, spending their lives breaking down dead plant material in the soil and leaf litter. They're quite small compared to the larger, more conspicuous millipedes you might find under logs.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Cylindrical and thread-like, much thinner than the chunky pill millipedes or larger garden millipedes you might know

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small - easily overlooked among soil particles and requiring close inspection to spot

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Moves with the characteristic millipede wave-like motion, but much more delicate than larger species

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale to light brown coloration that helps it blend in with decomposing organic matter

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Found deep in soil layers and decomposing leaf litter rather than under logs or stones

habitat: Look for winterchill millipedes in rich, moist forest soils throughout New England's deciduous and mixed woodlands. They prefer areas with deep leaf litter and well-decomposed organic matter, often several inches below the surface. You're most likely to encounter them when digging in garden soil or sifting through the deeper layers of forest duff.

seasonality.spring: Active in warming soils as snow melts, often found when turning over garden beds or raking away old leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Present but may move deeper into soil to avoid surface heat and drying, making them harder to spot during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Becomes more active as temperatures cool and fresh leaf litter provides new food sources for decomposition.
seasonality.winter: Remarkably, this species remains active even in cold weather when most other millipedes become dormant, living up to its "winterchill" name.

funFact: This millipede is so rare in New England that it's only been documented once in the entire region - making any sighting a genuine scientific treasure that could help researchers understand its true distribution and habitat needs!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for small earthworms, but millipedes have distinct segments with visible legs along their sides, while earthworms are smooth and legless. Remember: if it has tiny legs visible along its body, it's a millipede!
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of documented sightings doesn't necessarily mean this species is endangered - it's more likely that these tiny soil-dwellers are simply overlooked by most naturalists who focus on larger, more conspicuous wildlife.
compareHints: Since this is the only winterchill millipede species documented in New England, compare it to other small soil millipedes in the chordeumatid group by looking for its particularly slender build and cold-weather activity. Most similar millipedes become inactive in winter, while C. blakei continues moving through soil even when temperatures drop significantly.
